topics.title: The reactivity series and reactions of metals with air, water and steam

cards.front: List the eight metals of the reactivity series in order, most reactive first.
cards.back: Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper.

cards.front: Which metals react with cold water, and what are the two products?
cards.back: Potassium, sodium and calcium. They give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

cards.front: Which metals react with steam, and what are the two products? Why is the answer not the hydroxide?
cards.back: Magnesium, zinc and iron. They give the metal oxide and hydrogen. Steam is hot enough to strip the water right down, so the oxide forms; the hydroxide only comes from cold water.

cards.front: What do you see when iron, magnesium and copper are each heated in air?
cards.back: Iron gives orange sparks; magnesium burns with a bright white light; copper glows red. Each leaves the metal oxide behind.

cards.front: In the metal-and-steam experiment, what is the damp mineral wool for, and how is the gas collected?
cards.back: Heating the damp mineral wool boils the water in it and supplies the steam. The hydrogen is collected over water, because hydrogen is insoluble in water.

cards.front: Finish the sentence: the reactivity of a metal is its tendency to …
cards.back: … form its positive ion, by losing its outer electrons. The more easily a metal loses them, the higher it sits in the series.

cards.front: Complete both: calcium + water → ______ + ______ , and magnesium + steam → ______ + ______ .
cards.back: Calcium hydroxide + hydrogen; magnesium oxide + hydrogen.

cards.front: Reactivity series
cards.back: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Cu (most to least reactive).

topics.title: Displacement reactions and extraction of metals from ores

cards.front: State the rule for displacement reactions of metals in one sentence.
cards.back: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.

cards.front: Give three observations when zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution.
cards.back: The blue solution fades to colourless, a brown solid forms on the zinc, and the temperature rises.

cards.front: Complete: zinc + copper(II) sulfate → ______ + ______ , and give the balanced symbol equation.
cards.back: Zinc sulfate + copper. In symbols, Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu.

cards.front: Write the balanced symbol equation for the thermite reaction, and say in one clause why it happens.
cards.back: 2Al + Fe2O3 → 2Fe + Al2O3, because aluminium is more reactive than iron and so takes the oxygen.

cards.front: What is an ore, and which ore gives iron and which gives aluminium?
cards.back: An ore is a rock holding enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile. Haematite gives iron; bauxite gives aluminium.

cards.front: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis while iron is extracted with carbon?
cards.back: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from aluminium oxide and electricity has to do it. Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon reduces iron(III) oxide to iron.

cards.front: How would you use a grid of metals and salt solutions to rank four metals, and what must you keep the same?
cards.back: Add each metal to each salt solution in a separate tube and record whether a reaction happens. A reaction means the added metal is more reactive than the one in solution. Keep the volume and concentration of solution and the size of the metal the same each time.

cards.front: Metal displacement (Zn + CuSO4)
cards.back: Blue solution fades / turns colourless, brown solid (copper) forms, temperature rises.

topics.title: Oxidation and reduction (oxygen, hydrogen and electron transfer)

cards.front: Give the three definitions of oxidation.
cards.back: Gaining oxygen. Losing hydrogen. Losing electrons.

cards.front: Give the three definitions of reduction.
cards.back: Loss of oxygen; gain of hydrogen; gain of electrons.

cards.front: What does redox mean? Both halves of the answer, please.
cards.back: Oxidation and reduction taking place in the same reaction.

cards.front: In $\ce{CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O}$, which substance is oxidised, which is reduced, and how do you know?
cards.back: The hydrogen is oxidised because it gains oxygen; the copper(II) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen.

cards.front: OIL RIG stands for …?
cards.back: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

cards.front: Write the half equation for an iron atom becoming an iron(III) ion, and say which side the electrons go on and why.
cards.back: Fe → Fe3+ + 3e-. The electrons are lost, so they go on the right, and the charges then match: 0 on the left, +3 − 3 = 0 on the right.

cards.front: Write the half equation for a copper(II) ion becoming a copper atom.
cards.back: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. The electrons are gained, so they go in with the reactants.

cards.front: What is a reducing agent, and what happens to it?
cards.back: The substance that reduces something else, by giving electrons away or taking oxygen off it. It is itself oxidised.

cards.front: Name the reducing agent in the blast furnace and say what it does.
cards.back: Carbon monoxide. It takes the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide, reducing it to iron, and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide.

cards.front: In $\ce{Zn + Cu^{2+} -> Zn^{2+} + Cu}$, name the species oxidised, the species reduced, and the two agents.
cards.back: The zinc is oxidised (it loses two electrons) and is the reducing agent. The copper(II) ions are reduced (they gain two electrons) and are the oxidising agent.

cards.front: Oxidation / reduction
cards.back: Oxidation: gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen or (Higher) loss of electrons. Reduction: loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen or (Higher) gain of electrons.

topics.title: Rusting, its prevention and the extraction of iron

cards.front: Give the chemical name of rust, in full, and the two conditions iron needs to form it.
cards.back: Hydrated iron(III) oxide. Iron needs both water and oxygen.

cards.front: In the rusting tubes experiment, what are the anhydrous calcium chloride and the layer of oil each for?
cards.back: The anhydrous calcium chloride is a drying agent that removes water from the air in the tube. The oil stops oxygen dissolving back into the boiled water.

cards.front: Name four barrier methods of preventing rusting, and say what galvanising is.
cards.back: Painting, oiling or greasing, plastic coating, and galvanising. Galvanising is coating the iron with zinc.

cards.front: Explain sacrificial protection in two steps, and say which verb goes with the protecting metal.
cards.back: A more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is attached to the iron, and because it gives up its electrons more readily it corrodes in place of the iron. The protecting metal corrodes; only iron rusts.

cards.front: Name the three solids charged into a blast furnace and the gas blasted in at the base.
cards.back: Haematite, coke and limestone go in at the top; hot air is blasted in at the base.

cards.front: Write the four blast-furnace equations in the order they happen.
cards.back: C + O2 → CO2; CO2 + C → 2CO; Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2; CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, then CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3.

cards.front: Which of the two liquids at the base of the furnace is tapped off higher up, and why? And why is iron used for bridges?
cards.back: The slag, because it is less dense than the molten iron and floats on it. Iron is used in bridges and structures because of its strength.

cards.front: Colour: Rust
cards.back: Hydrated iron(III) oxide (orange-brown)

cards.front: Equation: Iron extraction
cards.back: C + O2 -> CO2; CO2 + C -> 2CO; Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2; CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3

topics.title: Measuring rates of reaction and interpreting rate graphs

cards.front: Write the rule for the rate of a reaction measured as a gas volume, and give its unit.
cards.back: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken, in cm³/s.

cards.front: A reaction is followed by timing how long a printed cross takes to be hidden. What is the rule for the rate, and its unit?
cards.back: rate = 1 ÷ time, in s⁻¹.

cards.front: Name the three ways CCEA allows you to follow the rate of a reaction.
cards.back: Measure the change in mass on a balance, measure the volume of gas collected, or time how long a precipitate takes to form.

cards.front: A gas syringe is read every 10 s. How do you find the total volume of gas produced?
cards.back: Take the last reading, where the readings stop changing: on the graph it is the height of the flat stretch. Do not add the readings together, because each one is a running total.

cards.front: On a volume-against-time curve, what does the steepness tell you, and what does the flat part tell you?
cards.back: The steepness is the rate, so the reaction is fastest at the start. The flat part means the reaction has stopped because a reactant has been used up.

cards.front: The same mass of carbonate is used but the chips are crushed. Where does the new curve finish, and why?
cards.back: At the same height as the original curve, because the same mass of carbonate can only make the same amount of gas. It just gets there sooner.

cards.front: Name the two pieces of apparatus in the gas-collection method, in the words the mark scheme wants.
cards.back: A gas syringe measures the volume of gas, and the reaction takes place in a conical flask.

cards.front: What must every column heading of a results table carry, and what does that decide on the graph?
cards.back: Its unit, written as Time / s or Volume of gas / cm³. The axis labels are copied straight from the headings, and a missing axis unit is the commonest lost mark.

cards.front: rate of reaction
cards.back: rate = 1 / time

topics.title: Collision theory: temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts

cards.front: What is the activation energy?
cards.back: The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.

cards.front: What makes a collision between particles a successful one?
cards.back: The particles collide with energy at or above the activation energy, so they react instead of bouncing apart.

cards.front: Write the phrase the mark scheme wants at the end of every rate explanation.
cards.back: More (or fewer) successful collisions per unit time.

cards.front: Raising the temperature does two things to the collisions. What are they?
cards.back: The particles collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of the collisions have energy at or above the activation energy.

cards.front: Raising the concentration does only one thing to the collisions. What is it, and why only one?
cards.back: Collisions become more frequent, because there are more particles in the same volume. Their energy is unchanged, because they are not moving any faster.
keyWords: more particles in the same volume

cards.front: A cube of side 2 cm is cut into 8 equal cubes. What happens to the surface area, the volume and the rate?
cards.back: The surface area doubles from 24 to 48 cm², the volume stays at 8 cm³, so the surface area to volume ratio rises from 3 to 6 cm⁻¹ and the reaction is faster.

cards.front: What is a catalyst, and what kind of substance is usually used as one?
cards.back: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up. Transition metals and their compounds are often used.

cards.front: Name the catalyst used for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, and say what it looks like.
cards.back: Manganese(IV) oxide, a black powder.

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.back: It provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

cards.front: A catalyst is added. What happens to the energy change of the reaction, and to the total amount of product?
cards.back: Neither changes. The profile starts and finishes at the same levels, and the amounts of reactant decide the amount of product; only the activation energy and the time taken are different.

cards.front: A table gives the mass of a solid before and after a reaction. How do you tell whether it was the catalyst?
cards.back: Its mass is the same before and after, and the reaction was faster than without it. A catalyst is also absent from the balanced equation.

cards.front: On a reaction profile, which arrow is the activation energy and which is the energy change?
cards.back: Arrow (i) is the activation energy: the climb from the reactant level to the top of the hump. Arrow (ii) is the energy change: the gap between the reactant level and the product level.

cards.front: Catalyst
cards.back: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up.

topics.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

cards.front: What is a reversible reaction?
cards.back: One that can go in both directions: the reactants form the products, and the products can react to form the reactants again.

cards.front: What sign is used in place of the usual arrow in a reversible reaction, and why is it worth a mark?
cards.back: The reversible sign, a double arrow. It records that both reactions happen, so a single arrow is a different claim and earns nothing.

cards.front: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated. What is seen, what is formed, and what happens if water is added afterwards?
cards.back: Blue turns white and water is driven off, leaving anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. Adding water turns it blue again and gives out heat.

cards.front: Define dynamic equilibrium.
cards.back: In a closed system, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.

cards.front: At equilibrium, what is equal and what is constant?
cards.back: The rates of the two reactions are equal; the amounts of reactants and products are constant. The amounts are not equal to each other.

cards.front: Name the three conditions that can be altered to change the direction of a reversible reaction.
cards.back: Temperature, pressure and concentration.

cards.front: Why must a system be closed before it can reach a dynamic equilibrium?
cards.back: Nothing can enter or escape, so the products stay in the container and can react back. In an open container the product escapes and the reverse reaction never catches up.

cards.front: Why is the equilibrium called dynamic rather than still?
cards.back: Both reactions are still going at equilibrium, at the same rate as each other, so nothing has stopped even though nothing appears to change.

cards.front: Dynamic equilibrium
cards.back: In a closed system, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.

topics.title: Homologous series, hydrocarbons and the alkanes

cards.front: Give the four features of a homologous series.
cards.back: The same general formula, similar chemical properties, a gradation in physical properties, and successive members differing by a CH2 group.

cards.front: What is a hydrocarbon, and which word in the definition carries a mark of its own?
cards.back: A compound that consists of hydrogen and carbon only. The word only is the second mark.

cards.front: Give the general formula of the alkanes, and use it for an alkane with 7 carbon atoms.
cards.back: CnH2n+2, so 7 carbons give 2 × 7 + 2 = 16 hydrogens: C7H16.

cards.front: Name the first four alkanes in order, and give the molecular formula of each.
cards.back: Methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10.

cards.front: How do you check that a displayed formula you have drawn is right?
cards.back: Count the lines at every carbon atom: there must be exactly four, because carbon always forms four covalent bonds.

cards.front: What is the state of the first four alkanes at room temperature, and how do you know?
cards.back: All four are gases, because every one of their boiling points is below room temperature, 20 °C.

cards.front: Why do boiling points rise as you go along the alkane family?
cards.back: Each member has one more CH2, so the molecules are larger and attract each other more strongly, and more energy is needed to separate them.

cards.front: An alkane has 12 carbon atoms. What is wrong with writing its formula as C12H24+2?
cards.back: The arithmetic has not been finished. 2 × 12 + 2 = 26, so the formula is C12H26: a formula has one number after each element.

cards.front: What does a displayed formula show, and how is it different from a molecular formula?
cards.back: A displayed formula shows every atom and every bond drawn as a line; a molecular formula only counts the atoms of each element.

cards.front: How many hydrogens would you draw on the middle carbon of any alkane chain, and why?
cards.back: Two, because it has already used two of its four bonds joining the carbons on either side of it.

cards.front: Homologous series
cards.back: A family of organic molecules with the same general formula, similar chemical properties, a gradation in physical properties, differing by CH2.

cards.front: Hydrocarbon
cards.back: A compound consisting of hydrogen and carbon only.

cards.front: Alkanes
cards.back: CnH2n+2 (methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10)

topics.title: Crude oil, fractional distillation and cracking

cards.front: Give three things the specification says about crude oil.
cards.back: It is a finite resource, it is the main source of hydrocarbons, and it is the feedstock of the petrochemical industry.

cards.front: What are the fractions from crude oil mostly made of, and what is their general formula?
cards.back: Alkanes, with the general formula CnH2n+2.

cards.front: Describe fractional distillation in three steps.
cards.back: The crude oil is heated and the hydrocarbons evaporate; the vapours rise up a column that is hottest at the bottom; each fraction condenses where the temperature matches its boiling point.

cards.front: Name the seven fractions in order from the top of the column.
cards.back: refinery gases, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oils, bitumen.

cards.front: Kerosene and naphtha are the two fractions most often confused. What is each one used for?
cards.back: Kerosene is a fuel for aircraft; naphtha is used for making chemicals and plastics.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say a fraction leaves low down because it is heavy?
cards.back: Every fraction rises as a vapour. What decides the height is the boiling point: a long chain has a high boiling point and condenses as soon as the vapour cools a little.

cards.front: What is cracking, and what conditions does it need?
cards.back: It breaks long saturated hydrocarbons apart into shorter molecules that are worth more, some of them unsaturated alkenes. It needs heat and a catalyst.

cards.front: A 10-carbon alkane cracks into an alkene of 2 carbons and one other molecule. Give the formula of every substance in the equation.
Crude-oil fractions (top to bottom)
cards.back: Refinery gases, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oils, bitumen.

topics.title: Complete and incomplete combustion; pollution from fuels

cards.front: Methane burns completely in oxygen. Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation.
cards.back: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O.

cards.front: What is produced when a hydrocarbon burns in a limited supply of oxygen?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide and water, and sometimes carbon, seen as soot.

cards.front: Give the test and the full result for carbon dioxide.
cards.back: Bubble the gas through limewater: the colourless solution turns milky. Colourless, not clear.

cards.front: Give the test and the full result for water.
cards.back: Add anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: it turns from white to blue.

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide toxic?
cards.back: It combines with haemoglobin in the blood, so the blood can carry less oxygen.

cards.front: What does carbon dioxide from burning fuels cause, and what does that lead to?
cards.back: The greenhouse effect, which causes climate change, sea-level rise and flooding.

cards.front: Where does the sulfur dioxide from a power station come from, and what does it cause?
cards.back: From sulfur impurities in the fuel. It causes acid rain, which damages buildings, destroys vegetation and kills fish.

cards.front: In what order do you balance a combustion equation, and why?
cards.back: Carbons first, then hydrogens, then oxygen last, because oxygen appears in both products so its count is only fixed once they are.

cards.front: Equation: Complete combustion of methane
cards.back: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O

topics.title: Alkenes, functional groups, addition reactions and the bromine-water test

cards.front: Give the general formula of the alkenes, and say how it differs from the alkanes'.
cards.back: CnH2n. It has two hydrogens fewer than CnH2n+2, because the second carbon-to-carbon bond uses two bonding positions.

cards.front: Name the four alkenes on the specification and give the formula of each.
cards.back: Ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, but-1-ene and but-2-ene, both C4H8.

cards.front: But-1-ene and but-2-ene are both C4H8. How do they differ?
cards.back: In where the double bond sits: between carbons 1 and 2 in but-1-ene, and between carbons 2 and 3 in but-2-ene.

cards.front: What is a functional group, and what are the groups for alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids?
cards.back: The reactive group in a molecule. Alkenes have C=C, alcohols have OH, and carboxylic acids have COOH.

cards.front: A question asks you to circle the functional group of an alkene. What exactly goes inside the circle?
cards.back: The two carbons and the double bond between them, and no hydrogen atoms.

cards.front: Give the test for a carbon-to-carbon double bond, with both results in the words the scheme wants.
cards.back: Shake with bromine water: with an alkene it goes from orange to colourless, and with an alkane there is no change. Colourless, never clear.

cards.front: Why are the alkanes less reactive than the alkenes, the alcohols and the carboxylic acids?
cards.back: Because the alkanes have no functional group, so there is no reactive part for anything to attack.

cards.front: Give the three addition reactions of ethene the specification lists, with their products.
cards.back: With bromine, giving C2H4Br2; with hydrogen, giving ethane; and with steam, giving ethanol.

cards.front: What happens to the double bond in an addition reaction?
cards.back: One of the two bonds between the carbons opens, and an atom or group joins each carbon, so only one product forms.

cards.front: Ethene is turned into ethanol industrially. What must you call the other reactant, and why does the word matter?
cards.back: Steam. The water is present as a vapour at the temperature and pressure used, and the scheme asks for steam rather than water.

cards.front: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethene.
What are the products when an alkene burns in a limited supply of oxygen?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide and water, often with soot as well; an alkene burns with a smokier flame than the alkane of the same length.

cards.front: Test for C=C double bond (alkene)
cards.back: Bromine water changes from orange to colourless.

cards.front: Functional group
cards.back: A reactive group in a molecule (C=C alkenes, -OH alcohols, -COOH carboxylic acids).

cards.front: Alkenes
cards.back: CnH2n (ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, but-1-ene and but-2-ene C4H8)

topics.title: Addition polymerisation

cards.front: What is a monomer, and what is a polymer?
cards.back: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to others; a polymer is the very long chain molecule made when many monomers join.

cards.front: Give the full name of the process that turns ethene into poly(ethene).
cards.back: Addition polymerisation. Each of the two words carries a mark.

cards.front: How do you name the polymer made from a monomer? Give the two examples CCEA names.
cards.back: Write poly, then the monomer's name in brackets: ethene gives poly(ethene) and chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene).

cards.front: What is PVC called in a CCEA answer, and what is its monomer?
cards.back: Poly(chloroethene), made from chloroethene, whose older name is vinyl chloride.

cards.front: A drawn repeat unit must show four things. What are they?
cards.back: Square brackets; a bond passing through each bracket; a single bond between the two carbons; and n after the closing bracket.

cards.front: Why can alkenes form addition polymers when alkanes cannot?
cards.back: Alkenes have a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to other monomers; alkanes have only single bonds, all in use.

cards.front: How can you check a repeat unit you have drawn?
cards.back: It must contain exactly the same atoms as the monomer, and every carbon must show four bonds.

cards.front: How do you find the monomer from a section of polymer chain?
cards.back: Mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat, remove the bonds to the neighbours, and put the C=C back between the two carbons.

cards.front: Where does n appear in the equation for the polymerisation of ethene?
cards.back: Twice: in front of the monomer and after the closing bracket of the repeat unit.

cards.front: Give one use of poly(ethene) and one use of poly(chloroethene).
cards.back: Poly(ethene): carrier bags, bottles or cling film. Poly(chloroethene): window frames, drainpipes or the insulation on electric cables.

topics.title: Alcohols, their combustion and fermentation

cards.front: Give the general formula and the functional group of the alcohols.
cards.back: CnH2n+1OH, with the OH group as the functional group.

cards.front: Name the four alcohols CCEA lists, with their formulae and state at room temperature.
cards.back: Methanol CH3OH, ethanol C2H5OH, propan-1-ol C3H7OH and propan-2-ol C3H7OH; all four are liquids.

cards.front: How do propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol differ, and why does the number in the name matter?
cards.back: The OH is on an end carbon in propan-1-ol and on the middle carbon in propan-2-ol. The number is the only difference in the names, so propanol alone earns nothing.

cards.front: What are the products of the complete and the incomplete combustion of an alcohol?
cards.back: Complete: carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete: carbon monoxide and water, often with carbon (soot).

cards.front: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
cards.back: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O.

cards.front: Balancing the oxygen for a burning alcohol: what is the step a hydrocarbon never needs?
cards.back: Take off the oxygen atom the alcohol already carries before halving the count, so ethanol needs 3O2, not 3.5O2.

cards.front: How is ethanol made by fermentation? Give what goes in and the conditions.
cards.back: Sugar dissolved in water, with yeast added, kept warm (about 25–37 °C) and with air kept out (anaerobic). It gives ethanol and carbon dioxide.

cards.front: Why is fermentation kept warm but not hot?
cards.back: Warmth makes the yeast's enzymes work fast; too hot and the enzymes are denatured, so fermentation stops.

cards.front: Why is air kept out during fermentation?
cards.back: With oxygen the yeast respires aerobically and makes carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol.

cards.front: Give the test for carbon dioxide in the words that earn every mark.
cards.back: Bubble the gas through limewater: it turns from colourless to milky. Colourless, never clear.

cards.front: Alcohols
cards.back: CnH2n+1OH (methanol CH3OH, ethanol C2H5OH, propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol C3H7OH)

topics.title: Carboxylic acids as weak acids and their reactions

cards.front: Carboxylic acids
cards.back: Methanoic HCOOH, ethanoic CH3COOH, propanoic C2H5COOH, butanoic C3H7COOH

topics.title: Empirical formulae, hydrated salts and water of crystallisation

cards.front: Heating hydrated copper(II) sulfate
cards.back: Blue crystals turn to white powder; steam/condensation; reversible on adding water.

cards.front: Empirical formula
cards.back: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.

cards.front: Water of crystallisation
cards.back: Water molecules chemically bonded within the crystal structure of a hydrated salt.

cards.front: degree of hydration
cards.back: x = moles of water lost / moles of anhydrous salt (moles = mass / Mr for each)

topics.title: Concentration of solutions and atom economy

cards.front: Write the formula for concentration, with its units.
cards.back: Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³).

cards.front: To change a volume in cm³ into dm³, you …
cards.back: Divide by 1000, because 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.

cards.front: How do you find the moles of solute in a volume of solution of known concentration?
cards.back: Moles = concentration × volume, with the volume in dm³.

cards.front: Give the three lines for finding the mass of solute needed to make a solution.
cards.back: Moles = concentration × volume in dm³. Mr from the Data Leaflet. Mass = moles × Mr.

cards.front: Write the formula for atom economy.
cards.back: Atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100.

cards.front: Give a sustainable-development reason and an economic reason for wanting a high atom economy.
cards.back: Sustainable development: fewer raw materials are used up and less waste is made. Economic: less money is spent on raw materials and on getting rid of waste.

cards.front: Why does 'it uses less energy' earn nothing when you are asked why a preparation is not sustainable?
cards.back: Atom economy is about atoms, not energy: the marks are for raw materials used up, waste made and the cost of both.

cards.front: What is the atom economy of a reaction that makes only one product, and why?
cards.back: 100%, because every atom of the reactants ends up in the desired product.

cards.front: What is the difference between atom economy and percentage yield?
cards.back: Atom economy comes from the balanced equation: the mass of the desired product over the total mass of products. Percentage yield comes from an experiment: the actual mass made over the most that could be made.

cards.front: What is the atom economy for making calcium oxide by heating calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂?
cards.back: 56%: calcium oxide is 56 out of a total product mass of 56 + 44 = 100.

cards.front: Your atom economy comes out at 212%. What has gone wrong?
cards.back: The fraction is upside down: put the desired mass on top and the total mass of products underneath. An atom economy can never be more than 100%.

cards.front: concentration
cards.back: concentration = moles / volume

cards.front: atom economy
cards.back: atom economy = (mass of desired product / total mass of products) x 100

topics.title: Electrolysis of molten salts and electrode half equations

cards.front: What is electrolysis?
cards.back: The decomposition of a liquid electrolyte by a direct electric current.

cards.front: Define an electrolyte.
cards.back: A liquid or solution that conducts electricity and is decomposed by it.

cards.front: The anode is the ______ electrode and the cathode is the ______ electrode.
cards.back: Positive; negative. (PANIC: Positive is Anode, Negative Is Cathode.)

cards.front: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved before it can be electrolysed?
cards.back: So that its ions are free to move and carry charge; in the solid they are held in a lattice.

cards.front: What is an inert electrode, and why is graphite used?
cards.back: One that takes no part in the reactions. Graphite is inert, conducts electricity and has a high melting point.

cards.front: Molten lead(II) bromide: the product and what you see at each electrode?
cards.back: Cathode: lead, a grey liquid. Anode: bromine, bubbles of a red-brown gas.

cards.front: Molten lithium chloride: the product and what you see at each electrode?
cards.back: Cathode: lithium, a silvery-grey bead. Anode: chlorine, bubbles of a green gas.

cards.front: Write the half equation at the cathode for molten lead(II) bromide.
cards.back: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (two electrons gained, on the left).

cards.front: Write the half equation at the anode for molten lead(II) bromide.
cards.back: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (bromine is a molecule; two electrons lost, on the right).

cards.front: A red-brown gas forms at the anode. Is it bromide or bromine?
cards.back: Bromine. Bromide is the ion that arrives; bromine is the element that forms.

cards.front: What carries the charge through a molten salt: electrons or ions?
cards.back: Ions. Electrons carry the current only in the wires and the electrodes.

cards.front: Why is the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide done in a fume cupboard?
cards.back: Because bromine, formed at the anode, is toxic.

cards.front: Electrolysis of molten lithium chloride
cards.back: Cathode: silvery lithium; anode: pale green chlorine gas.

cards.front: Electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide
cards.back: Cathode: silvery-grey bead of lead; anode: red-brown bromine vapour.

cards.front: Electrolysis
cards.back: The decomposition of a molten or dissolved ionic compound by passing electricity through it.

topics.title: Industrial extraction and recycling of aluminium

cards.front: Equation: Aluminium electrolysis half equations
cards.back: Al3+ + 3e- -> Al (cathode); 2O2- -> O2 + 4e- (anode); C + O2 -> CO2 at the anode

topics.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, reaction profiles and bond energies

cards.front: What do exothermic and endothermic mean, and what does the thermometer do in each?
cards.back: Exothermic: heat is given out, so the temperature rises. Endothermic: heat is taken in, so the temperature falls.

cards.front: A question asks for an observation. Is 'exothermic' an acceptable answer?
cards.back: No. An observation is what you see or feel: the temperature rose, or the tube became hot. Exothermic is the conclusion drawn from it.

cards.front: What is the activation energy?
cards.back: The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.

cards.front: On a reaction profile, what are the four things a four-mark question wants you to get right?
cards.back: One smooth reaction-pathway line; the product level on the correct side; the activation energy arrow from the reactant level to the top of the hump; the energy-change arrow between the two levels.

cards.front: What happens to energy when a bond is broken, and when a bond is made?
cards.back: Breaking a bond takes energy in; making a bond gives energy out.

cards.front: Write the rule for the energy change of a reaction from bond energies.
cards.back: Energy change = energy taken in to break bonds − energy given out when bonds are made.

cards.front: Your bond-energy answer comes out negative. What does that mean, and what must you not leave off?
cards.back: Negative means more energy was given out than taken in, so the reaction is exothermic. The minus sign must be written on the answer line.

cards.front: A reaction has an energy change of −184 kJ. What is the energy change for the reverse reaction, and what kind of reaction is that?
cards.back: +184 kJ: the same size with the opposite sign, so the reverse reaction is endothermic.

cards.front: Activation energy
cards.back: The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.

cards.front: Exothermic / endothermic
cards.back: Exothermic: heat is given out. Endothermic: heat is taken in.

cards.front: energy change from bond energies
cards.back: energy change = energy taken in to break bonds - energy released when bonds form

topics.title: The atmosphere, nitrogen and the ammonia test

cards.front: Test for Ammonia
cards.back: Glass rod dipped in concentrated hydrochloric acid gives white smoke (ammonium chloride).

cards.front: Atmosphere
cards.back: About 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.03-0.04% carbon dioxide, 1% argon, traces of other noble gases, variable water vapour.

topics.title: Preparing hydrogen and oxygen; reactions of elements with oxygen

cards.front: Test for Oxygen
cards.back: Relights a glowing splint (Prescribed Practical C6 "tests" for the gases).

topics.title: Preparing carbon dioxide and its reactions with water and limewater

cards.front: Equation: Carbon dioxide with limewater
cards.back: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O; then CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2 with excess CO2
